newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch Dakota ditches in sea - all 32 aboard die.
newsitem.headline: Dutch Dakota ditches in sea - all 32 aboard die.

text.p: All 32 people on board a 55-year-old DC-3 Dakota aircraft died on Wednesday when it ditched into the North Sea near the Dutch naval town of Den Helder after reporting engine trouble, the coastguard said.

The World War Two vintage aircraft, carrying 26 passengers and six crew, was owned by the Dutch Dakota Association and was carrying members and sponsors on the return leg of pleasure trip from Amsterdam to Texel, an island just off the Dutch coast.
"We have recovered 31 bodies, one survivor who was taken to hospital has since died," said coastguard spokesman Pieter Paap, confirming 32 people were on the flight.

He said the search and rescue operation around the plane, lodged on a sandbank in 1.50 metres (five feet) of water, had been called off and efforts on Thursday would concentrate on recovering the wreckage.
The aircraft, used mainly for displays and pleasure trips, ditched into the sea east of Den Helder at 4:45 p.m. (1445 GMT), after the pilot radioed that he had engine trouble.
"He had indicated that he wanted to make an emergency landing at the naval airbase De Kooy. He had a problem with one engine and somehow something went wrong," a navy spokesman said.

Eyewitnesses spoke of seeing apparently lifeless bodies still strapped into their seats, drifting in the water near the crash site as 10 lifeboats, two helicopters and a flotilla of fishing vessels converged on the scene.
Anne Groeneveld, founder and president of the DDA said the aircraft was in perfect technical condition and had recently been checked by the national civial aviation authority.
"At the moment I have no reason to suspect that there was a technical problem, but we'll only know that once an investigation has been held," he told a news conference.
Groeneveld's organisation is a band of pilots and aviation enthusiasts which bought the DC-3 in 1983 for 300,000 guilders ($160,000) and lovingly restored it to its former glory.
As well as air show displays, it was used for pleasure flights for DDA members and corporate sponsors, regularly carrying up to 32 passengers and six crew.
Paap said an investigation would be opened by the Dutch airforce as soon as possible.
Eleven thousand Dakotas were built between 1935 and 1948, making it the most prolific transport aircraft ever produced.
About 1,000 of them are believed to be still flying with air forces, commercially or for fun.

Made by the Douglas Aircraft Corporation, the Dakota was equipped with two 1,200-horsepower Pratt and Whitney propeller engines which gave it a cruising speed of about 200 km an hour (125 miles an hour).

The Dakota, a symbol to the Dutch of liberation after World War Two, dominated the skies in the 1930s and 1940s, ferrying supplies during the Normandy landings in France in 1944 and the Berlin airlift of 1948.

The name, experts say, derives from a shortening of the plane's original title the Douglas Aircraft Corporation Transport Aircraft (DACoTA). This was soon corrupted to Dakota, after the U.S. states, by pilots of Britain's Royal Air Force.
